title: Capstone: Chavruta — Present a Sugya, Its Argument and Its Mercy
bigQuestion: What does it take to read a sugya with a partner, argue its sides fairly and say clearly what it protects?

story.title: Two Sides of One Page
story.kicker: Two students take opposite sides of a Talmud passage and end up agreeing on what it is about.
paragraphs: Maya and Luis stand at the front of the room with one printed page between them. It is Bava Metzia 21a-b, on lost objects, in paraphrase. Maya argues that a finder may keep scattered coins. Luis argues that the owner still has a claim. The class has a rubric and a timer.

They do not shout. Maya reads the Mishnah's line and explains the idea of an owner who has given up hope, called *yiush* in the Gemara. Luis answers with an objection the Gemara itself raises: what if the owner does not yet know the coins are gone? They trade the page back and forth, the way the rabbis traded proofs.

Near the end, Maya says something the class did not expect. She says both of them are really arguing about the same thing: how to protect a person who loses something without punishing the person who finds it. Luis nods. Their thesis is that the sugya weighs the owner's claim against the finder's honesty.

This is the capstone. You will choose a sugya, read it with a partner in *chavruta*, map its moves, bring in commentators and a modern reader, and present both sides. The goal is not to win. It is to show the argument and the mercy on the page.
story.think: Why might two students who argue opposite sides end up agreeing on what a passage is about?

lessons.title: Choosing Your Sugya
lessons.mainIdea: A good capstone sugya is short, has a clear dispute and asks what a ruling protects.
reading: This course has read many sugyot: lost objects in Bava Metzia, workers' wages, saving a life, honoring parents in Kiddushin, and 'these and those' in Eruvin 13b. Any of them can be a capstone. You may also choose another passage, as long as you can cite tractate and page and find a translation.

Choose for three things. First, length: one sugya, often half a page to a full daf. Second, a clear dispute, with named sides such as Abaye and Rava or Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Third, stakes: a person the ruling protects, such as the worker, the finder, the owner or a person in danger.

Translations differ in status. Michael Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud (1896-1903) is public domain but abridged and uneven, so check it against a modern edition. The Soncino (1935-52), Steinsaltz and Sefaria's William Davidson edition are not public domain; use them to read, and paraphrase them in your own words when you present.

no longer under copyright, so it may be quoted and shared freely
to restate a passage in your own words while keeping its meaning

lessons.title: Reading in Chavruta
lessons.mainIdea: Chavruta is paired study in which partners read aloud, question each other and argue toward understanding.
reading: *Chavruta* comes from the Aramaic word for friend or companion. It means study in pairs. In many yeshivas and batei midrash, study halls, the room is loud with pairs reading aloud and arguing. The Talmud itself praises this. In Taanit 23a, Rava is quoted: either chavruta or death.

Taanit 7a applies Proverbs 27:17, iron sharpens iron, to students. Just as one iron blade sharpens another, the Gemara says, two scholars sharpen each other in law. Berakhot 63b warns that those who study alone grow foolish. The ideal is not a lecture but a partner.

In practice, partners take turns. One reads a line aloud and explains it. The other asks: who is speaking, what is the question, what is the proof? Then they switch. When they disagree, they return to the text. The rule of the room is to argue with ideas, never to attack the person.

words.d: study in pairs; from the Aramaic word for friend or companion
a study hall where Torah and Talmud are studied; plural batei midrash
a school devoted to traditional Jewish study, especially Talmud

look.title: Iron Sharpens Iron
look.text: Why are words of Torah compared to iron? Because as one iron sharpens another, so two scholars sharpen each other in the study of law.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 7a, on Proverbs 27:17, paraphrased (compare the Soncino translation, 1938)
look.prompt: What does the image of two blades suggest about how partners should disagree?

check.q: What does 'chavruta' mean?
choices: The anonymous voice of the Gemara
Study in pairs, from the word for companion
check.why: Chavruta, from the Aramaic for companion, is paired study.

check.q: Which verse does Taanit 7a apply to two scholars?
choices: Deuteronomy 30:12, it is not in heaven
check.why: Taanit 7a reads Proverbs 27:17 as scholars sharpening each other.

check.q: What is the main rule for disagreement in chavruta?

check.why: Chavruta argues over the text itself while respecting the partner.

lessons.title: Map the Moves
lessons.mainIdea: Before arguing, partners map the sugya: Mishnah, question, proof, objection, answer and ruling.
reading: Start with the *Mishnah* or baraita the sugya discusses. Write it in one sentence. Then list each move the Gemara makes. Label it: question, proof, objection, answer, story or ruling. Mark each speaker by name or as the anonymous voice. Keep the map on one sheet so both partners can see it.

Use the signal words you have learned. 'Ta shema' brings a proof. 'Metivei' raises an objection. 'Teyku', let it stand, marks a question left unresolved. 'Hilkheta' gives the ruling. When no signal appears, ask what job the line is doing. Circle each signal word you find on the page.

A map for Bava Metzia 21a might have eight to twelve moves. Do not try to capture every word. Capture the path of the argument. Your map is the backbone of your presentation, and the rubric gives it real weight. A clear map also helps your listeners follow along.

words.d: an Aramaic word closing a question the Gemara leaves unresolved
Aramaic for 'they objected'; it introduces a challenge from a source
one step in a sugya's argument, such as a question, proof or objection

look.title: Label Each Line
look.text: Line 1: The Mishnah says scattered coins belong to the finder. Line 2: Why? Because the owner has given up hope. Line 3: But he may not know he lost them yet! Line 4: A person often touches his purse, so he knows. Line 5: The law follows this.
look.prompt: Label each line as source, question, answer, objection or ruling. Which line is the key move?

check.q: What does 'teyku' signal?
check.why: Teyku closes a question the Gemara cannot settle.

check.q: What should a sugya map start with?
choices: The Mishnah or baraita the sugya discusses
check.why: The Gemara is built on a source text, so the map begins there.

check.q: What does 'metivei' introduce?
check.why: Metivei, they objected, launches a challenge.

lessons.title: Rashi at Your Elbow
lessons.mainIdea: Rashi's commentary explains the plain sense of each line and sits beside the Gemara on the printed page.
reading: Rashi, Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, lived in Troyes, France, from 1040 to 1105. His commentary on the Talmud explains words, fills in missing steps and tells the reader who is speaking. In the standard printed page, it runs in a column on the inner side, next to the binding.

Students often say they read the Gemara 'with Rashi.' When a line is unclear, Rashi supplies a short gloss. He might say what a coin was, what a verse proves or why an objection works. Many learners treat him as a patient tutor at their elbow. Each gloss is short and to the point.

For your capstone, find one place where Rashi explains a key move. Paraphrase what he says and name the line. Rashi's commentary is not a public-domain English text you can quote freely, so present it in your own words with the tractate, page and 'Rashi, s.v.' plus the word he comments on.

words.d: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040-1105) of Troyes, France, the most widely read commentator on the Talmud
a short explanation of a word or line
short for Latin 'sub verbo', 'under the word'; tells which words a commentator is explaining

check.q: Where did Rashi live?
check.why: Rashi lived and taught in Troyes, France, 1040-1105.

check.q: What does 's.v.' tell a reader in a citation to Rashi?

lessons.title: Tosafot Push Back
lessons.mainIdea: Tosafot compare passages across the Talmud and often challenge Rashi, modeling respectful disagreement.
reading: *Tosafot*, meaning 'additions', are comments by medieval scholars in France and Germany, many of them Rashi's own descendants and students. They were active from the twelfth into the fourteenth century. Their notes run on the outer side of the printed page.

Where Rashi explains one line, Tosafot often ask how this sugya fits with another page. They notice contradictions and try to resolve them. Many times they begin by quoting Rashi, then write, in effect, 'this is hard,' and give another reading. Rashi's grandson Rabbeinu Tam was one of the best known.

In your capstone, one Tosafot comment, paraphrased, can show a second reading of your sugya. It shows that disagreement continued long after the Gemara was complete. Like Beit Hillel, Tosafot usually state the view they question before offering their own.

words.d: 'additions'; medieval comments by scholars in France and Germany, printed on the outer margin
Rabbi Jacob ben Meir (c. 1100-1171), Rashi's grandson and a leading Tosafist
two statements that seem to disagree; Tosafot often try to reconcile them

look.title: Rashi and Tosafot on One Line
look.text: Imagine a line where Rashi says a rule applies only in a city. Tosafot quote Rashi, then point to another tractate where the same rule applies in a field too. They offer a different reading that fits both pages.
look.prompt: How is Tosafot's move like an objection in the Gemara? How is it also respectful of Rashi?

check.q: What does 'Tosafot' mean?
check.why: Tosafot means 'additions', comments added to the Talmud and Rashi.

check.q: What is a typical move of Tosafot?
choices: Comparing one sugya with another and resolving contradictions
check.why: Tosafot range across the Talmud to find and resolve tensions.

check.q: Who was Rabbeinu Tam?
choices: A tanna of the first century
Rashi's grandson and a leading Tosafist
check.why: Rabbi Jacob ben Meir, Rabbeinu Tam, was Rashi's grandson and a major Tosafist.

lessons.title: One Modern Reader
lessons.mainIdea: A modern reader, religious or academic, shows how the sugya is understood and used today.
reading: Your capstone also brings in one modern reader. Rabbi Adin Steinsaltz (1937-2020) translated and explained the whole Talmud in Hebrew and later English, aiming to open the page to beginners. His notes often explain history, objects and plants. Other editions and translations exist as well.

Academic readers ask different questions. David Weiss Halivni studied how the anonymous layer was built. Daniel Boyarin and others read aggadah as literature and culture. Women scholars and teachers, including those at women's batei midrash, have raised questions earlier readers left aside.

Pick one reader and say what their approach does. Does it explain the plain sense, trace history, or draw an ethical lesson? Attribute every claim: 'Steinsaltz explains…', 'Halivni argues…'. Do not present any reader's view as the only one. Let each reader speak in their own terms.

words.d: an Israeli rabbi (1937-2020) who translated and explained the whole Babylonian Talmud
study of the Talmud using history, language and manuscripts, without deciding religious questions
to name who holds a view, such as 'Rashi explains' or 'Halivni argues'

look.title: Three Readers, One Line

look.prompt: Write one sentence for each reader, attributed. Which approach fits your capstone sugya best, and why?

lessons.title: A Thesis About Argument and Mercy
lessons.mainIdea: A strong thesis names what the argument decides and what the ruling protects, with a citation.
reading: A thesis is one or two sentences your whole presentation defends. For this capstone it has two parts. First, what the argument decides. Second, what the ruling protects. For example: 'Bava Metzia 21b decides that a finder may keep coins once the owner has given up hope, and so protects both the owner's claim and the finder's honesty.'

Cite exactly: tractate, folio and side, like Bava Metzia 21b or Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:1. Name the translation you read, such as Rodkinson (1896-1903) or the Soncino (1935-52). If you paraphrase, say so. Paraphrase any translation that is not public domain, and mark it clearly.

Keep the minority view in your thesis or right after it. The Talmud does. A thesis that ignores the losing side misses half the page. Your partner will test this when they take the other side. A fair thesis makes room for the other side from the start.

words.d: the main claim a presentation or essay argues for
the exact place a text comes from, such as tractate, folio and side
one leaf of a book with two sides; in the Talmud, side a and side b

look.title: Strong or Weak?
look.text: Thesis A: 'Kiddushin is about parents.' Thesis B: 'Kiddushin 32a decides that a parent's needs are paid from the parent's money, protecting a poor child while later codes still require a child with means to help.'

choices: The date and the author's hometown

check.q: Why include the minority view near your thesis?

lessons.title: Presenting With Your Partner
lessons.mainIdea: In the presentation, partners take opposite sides, then state together what the sugya is about.
reading: Each pair gets about ten minutes. One partner presents the ruling side, the other the minority or objecting side. Each reads the key line, explains its moves and cites the page. Then you switch roles for one exchange, so each partner argues both ways.

End together. State your shared thesis: what the argument decides and what it protects. Name one commentator, Rashi or Tosafot in paraphrase, and one modern reader. Close with an open question the page leaves for later readers. Keep this closing short and clear.

The rubric below shows how points are shared. Notice that the map of moves and fair treatment of both sides carry the most weight. Winning is not on the rubric. Clear, respectful argument is. Fairness to both sides is what earns the most points here.

words.d: a scoring guide that shows what a project is judged on and how much each part counts
one round in which a speaker makes a point and the partner answers

lessons.title: Studying a Sacred Text in a Public School
lessons.mainIdea: Studying the Talmud in a public school means describing what readers believe, not telling anyone what to believe.
reading: In Abington School District v. Schempp (1963), the U.S. Supreme Court ruled against required Bible reading as a devotional act in public schools. The same decision said that studying religion objectively, as part of a secular education, is allowed. This course follows that line.

That is why every belief in this course is attributed. 'Rabbinic tradition holds…', 'Rashi explains…', 'historians date…'. The course does not say whether the Oral Torah came from Sinai or whether any ruling binds the reader. Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and academic readers each read the page their own way.

Close your capstone with a short reflection. What did you learn about argument, about mercy and about listening to a partner? Students of many backgrounds, and of none, have found that a page about lost coins or sleeping fathers can teach how to disagree well.

words.d: not religious; a public school's program is secular even when it studies religion
done as an act of worship rather than as study
describing fairly without taking a side on religious truth

lessons.title: Looking Back, Looking Ahead
lessons.mainIdea: The capstone gathers the course's threads: the page's moves, its mercy and a partner who disagrees well.
reading: Across this course you met the Mishnah (c. 200 CE), the Gemara of Babylonia (completed c. 500-600 CE), Rashi and Tosafot, codes like Maimonides and the Shulchan Arukh, and modern readers. You learned to cite a daf and to name a translation. You also practiced reading in pairs.

The Daf Yomi program, begun in 1923, has readers study one folio a day. A full cycle of about 2,711 folios takes about seven and a half years. In January 2020, tens of thousands filled MetLife Stadium in New Jersey to mark a completion, a Siyum HaShas. Readers in Chicago and around the world took part.

You do not need to finish the Talmud to use its method. Read the source. Map the moves. Hear the other side. Ask who is protected. That is the capstone, and it is also a skill you can carry into any argument. The page is waiting for the next pair of readers.
